**What you already know:** In P.1 and P.2 you learnt about accidents, safety and transport. In P.6 you study **Safety on the Road** — who uses the road, how each road user stays safe, the main road signs, traffic lights, safe crossing, and how road accidents are caused, prevented and why road safety matters.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: say what road safety and a road user are
name the road users and the safety rules for each of them
name and describe the three main types of road signs
say what the red, yellow and green traffic lights mean
describe a safe way of crossing a road
state the causes and effects of road accidents and how to prevent them

blocks.x: **Road safety** refers to the measures taken to prevent accidents and protect people using roads.
People who use roads are called **road users**.
Examples of road users:

items: Pedestrians
Drivers
Passengers
Cyclists
Motorcyclists
Animal handlers

blocks.x: 1. Pedestrians
A **pedestrian** is a person who walks along or crosses a road.
Safety rules for pedestrians:

items: Walk on the **right side of the road** where there is no footpath, facing oncoming traffic.
Use a **footpath or pavement** where it is provided.
Cross the road at a **zebra crossing, pedestrian crossing or other safe place**.
Look **right, left and right again** before crossing where traffic approaches from the right.
Do not run across the road.
Do not play on the road.
Obey traffic lights and road signs.
Wear bright or reflective clothing when walking at night.
Avoid using a phone or wearing earphones while crossing the road.
Hold young children's hands when crossing busy roads.

blocks.x: 2. Drivers
A **driver** is a person who controls and operates a vehicle.
Safety rules for drivers:

items: Obey traffic rules and road signs.
Drive at a safe speed.
Do not drive when drunk or under the influence of drugs.
Do not use a mobile phone while driving.
Wear a seat belt.
Keep the vehicle in good mechanical condition.
Do not overload the vehicle.
Give way to pedestrians at designated crossings.
Keep a safe distance from other vehicles.
Do not overtake where it is dangerous.
Use indicators when turning or changing lanes.

blocks.x: 3. Passengers
A **passenger** is a person travelling in a vehicle but is not controlling it.
Safety rules for passengers:

items: Wear a seat belt where one is provided.
Sit properly in the vehicle.
Do not distract the driver.
Do not put your head or hands outside the vehicle.
Do not jump on or off a moving vehicle.
Do not stand in a moving vehicle unless the vehicle is designed for standing passengers.
Do not overload the vehicle.
Children should use appropriate child restraints where available.

blocks.x: 4. Cyclists
A **cyclist** is a person who rides a bicycle.
Safety rules for cyclists:

items: Wear a properly fitted helmet.
Ride on the correct side of the road.
Obey traffic signs and signals.
Use hand signals when turning.
Keep the bicycle in good condition.
Use lights or reflectors when riding at night.
Do not carry too many passengers.
Do not ride while using a mobile phone.
Avoid riding at excessive speed.
Keep both hands available for controlling the bicycle when necessary.

blocks.x: 5. Motorcyclists
A **motorcyclist** is a person who rides a motorcycle.
Safety rules for motorcyclists:

items: Wear a properly fitted helmet.
Obey traffic rules and road signs.
Ride at a safe speed.
Keep the motorcycle in good condition.
Do not ride under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

Do not carry more passengers than the motorcycle is designed to carry.
Use indicators when turning.
Wear visible or reflective clothing, especially at night.

**What you already know:** In lower classes you have discussed topics and given your opinions in class. In P.6 you learn the **formal way of discussing a topic** — the debate — with its sides, its people, its rules and its language.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: say what a debate, a motion, a proposition and an opposition are
name the people who take part in a debate and the work of each
tell the types, parts and rules of a debate
prepare for a debate and give points for or against a motion

blocks.x: A **debate** is a formal discussion in which people give different opinions about a particular topic or motion.
A debate normally has **two sides**:

items: The **proposing side (for)** supports the motion.
The **opposing side (against)** disagrees with the motion.

sections.title: IMPORTANT TERMS USED IN A DEBATE

blocks.x: 1. Motion
A **motion** is the statement or topic being debated.
**Example:** "Pupils should be allowed to use mobile phones at school."
2. Proposition
The **proposition** is the side that supports the motion.
3. Opposition
The **opposition** is the side that disagrees with the motion.
4. Speaker
A **speaker** is a person who presents ideas during a debate.
5. Chairperson
The **chairperson** is the person who controls and guides the debate.
6. Timekeeper
A **timekeeper** is a person who keeps track of the time given to each speaker.
7. Audience
The **audience** consists of people who listen to the debate.
1. Formal Debate
This is a debate that follows specific rules and procedures.
Examples include:

items: School debates
Parliamentary debates
Inter-school debates

blocks.x: 2. Informal Debate
This is a less organised discussion where people exchange different opinions about an issue.
A debate normally has the following parts:

items: Introduction of the motion
Introduction of the speakers
Presentation of arguments for the motion
Presentation of arguments against the motion
Rebuttal of opposing arguments
Conclusion
Decision or voting

blocks.x: During a debate, participants should:

Follow the instructions of the chairperson.
Keep within the time given.
Address the chairperson properly.
Avoid interrupting another speaker.
Stay focused on the motion.

**What you already know:** You can name the members of your family. In P.6 you learn the **full family vocabulary in English** — the types of families, every family member and relationship, what a family does, and how good relationships are built and kept.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

blocks.x: A **family** is a group of people related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together or care for one another.
1. Nuclear Family
A **nuclear family** consists of a father, mother and their children.
2. Extended Family
An **extended family** consists of parents, children and other relatives such as grandparents, uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces and cousins.
3. Single-parent Family
A **single-parent family** is a family in which children are raised by one parent.
4. Child-headed Family
A **child-headed family** is a family where children live without adult parents or guardians and the oldest child takes responsibility for the younger children.

**What you already know:** You have seen a dictionary in class. In P.6 you learn **how to use it properly** — alphabetical order, guide words, meanings, pronunciation, abbreviations and labels — and the grammar of **question tags, opposites and superlatives**.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: arrange words in alphabetical order
use guide words to find a word quickly
find the meaning, spelling, pronunciation and part of speech of a word
understand the abbreviations and labels used in a dictionary
use a thesaurus to find words of similar meaning
use question tags, opposites and superlative forms

blocks.x: **Dictionary:** A book that lists words in alphabetical order and gives their meanings, spellings, pronunciations and other information.
What a dictionary tells you about a word

items: Its **spelling**
Its **meaning** (sometimes several meanings)
Its **pronunciation** and the **stress** — which part is said more strongly
Its **part of speech** — noun, verb, adjective and so on
Its **plural** or other forms
Its **origin**, and sometimes an **example sentence**

blocks.x: **Thesaurus:** A book that gives words of **similar meaning (synonyms)** and opposite meaning (antonyms).
The dictionary follows the **alphabet: A B C D E … Z**.
**The rule:** compare the **first letters**. If they are the same, compare the **second**, then the **third**, and so on.
Worked examples
*Notice:* **peach** comes **before** **people**, and **people** comes **after** **peach**, because *pea…* comes before *peo…* (a before o).
**Guide words:** The two words printed at the top of a dictionary page. The one on the left is the **first** word on that page, and the one on the right is the **last**.
**How to use them:** if the guide words are **market — mask**, then *marry, marsh* and *martin* are on that page, but *marble* (before) and *mast* (after) are not.

sections.title: 4. OTHER THINGS IN A DICTIONARY ENTRY

blocks.x: Parts of speech and their short forms
A sample entry
**kind** /kaɪnd/ *adj.* 1. gentle and caring towards others: *She is **kind** to animals.* 2. *n.* a type or sort: *What **kind** of book is it?* — **kindly** *adv.* · **kindness** *n.*
From this entry you learn the spelling, the pronunciation, that the word can be an **adjective** or a **noun**, two meanings, an example, and two related words.
Labels you may meet
**formal / informal** · **old-fashioned** · **British / American** · **slang** · **foreign words** taken into English, such as *safari*, *veranda*, *matooke* and *sauna*.
Acronyms and abbreviations
An **acronym** is a word made from the first letters of other words: **UNEB**, **NEMA**, **UWA**, **NGO**, **AIDS**. Many dictionaries list them too.
(a) Question tags
A short question added to a statement. **Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag.**
(b) Opposites (antonyms)
**By adding a prefix:** happy → **unhappy** · possible → **impossible** · legal → **illegal** · regular → **irregular** · agree → **disagree** · behave → **misbehave**.
(c) Superlative forms
**The rule:** use **-est** or **most** with **the**: *the **tallest** boy*, *the **most useful** book*. Never write "more taller" or "most tallest".
